claims.text: Standard synthesis of bulk HfNbTaTiZr yields polycrystalline specimens with typical defects.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr specimens contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework augments conventional analytical methods with machine-learned, defect-aware corrections trained on experimental conductivity data.
Impurity and boundary scattering dominate conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr from approximately 0 to 200 K.
Phonon interactions and defect scattering are both significant in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen-induced defects and other imperfections act as scattering centers that modify carrier transport.
Accounting explicitly for oxygen-induced scattering and temperature-dependent carrier interactions corrects estimates made under defect-free assumptions.
The defect-aware model will match measured conductivity more closely than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models in both specified temperature regimes.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical models underestimate the effect of defect and impurity scattering.
The defect-aware approach will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to conventional analytical models in the 0–200 K regime.
The defect-aware approach will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to conventional analytical models in the 300–1200 K regime.
The proposed applicability domain is bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen levels around 1 wt.% over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model may require recalibration or lose accuracy at substantially higher impurity levels or in the untested intermediate-temperature range.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with sample-specific defect distributions and measurement conditions.
Failure to reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% in both temperature regimes would falsify the hypothesis.
Systematic agreement of measured conductivity with the perfect-crystal model would falsify the hypothesis.
